volumes.title: The Spring Below Cold Tarn
volumes.text:
I am Barnaby Stile, forty years ferryman at Emberwick. I have carried people across the river Ember all my working life without once asking where it came from. Now the ferry is my nephew's, my knees still serve, and I mean to walk the whole river from its first trickle to the sea.

It begins, I find, as a wet place in the moss below Cold Tarn, high in the Northern Fells. No banks, no bed. You could stop it with your hat.

I have brought an old fly-box with twelve compartments, and my rule is one stone for each stretch of the walk. The first is a chip of grey granite from the spring itself, speckled black and sharp enough to scratch my thumb. The river has not yet had its way with it. We shall see what eighty miles can do.

volumes.title: Sharp Slate in Scree Beck
volumes.text:
Second day of my walk down the river Ember. Up here in the Fells it is called Scree Beck, and it is narrow enough to step across, though it makes the noise of something far grander.

Its bed is all slate, fallen from the crags above. Every piece is flat, dark and sharp at the corners. I turned over fifty and found not one rounded edge. These stones have only just arrived: frost split them from the crag, perhaps last winter, and the beck has not had time to roll them anywhere.

Into the second compartment of my fly-box goes a slate shaped like an arrowhead. A shepherd asked what I was looking for. "A round one," I said. He told me, kindly, that I was in the wrong valley for that, and gave me half his cheese.

volumes.title: The White Stone
volumes.text:
Where Whin Gill joins it, the young river Ember grows wide enough to need stepping stones. I, Barnaby Stile, late of the Emberwick ferry, crossed them with great dignity and one wet boot.

In the bank there, a white stripe as broad as my hand runs across the dark rock. It is a vein of quartz, where water once filled a crack and left crystal behind. The beck breaks lumps from it, and because quartz is harder than nearly everything round about, the white lumps last. I followed them for half a mile downstream, their corners only just beginning to blunt.

Stone three is milky quartz the size of a walnut. My knife will not scratch it; the blade leaves a grey line of its own steel instead. Of all the stones a river carries, I am told this is the one that goes the distance.

volumes.title: The Potholes at Hobb's Force
volumes.text:
Four days below its spring, the river Ember throws itself off a ledge. Hobb's Force is thirty feet of white water, and I stood in the spray long enough to wet my pipe past lighting.

At the foot of the fall the rock is drilled with holes, round as cooking pots and some as deep as my arm. I reached into one and brought up a handful of pebbles. Round! Properly round, like marbles. The fall spins them in the hole, day and night, and they grind the pot deeper while it grinds them smooth. A mill with no miller.

So my fourth compartment holds the first round stone of the walk: a grey-green ball no bigger than a hazelnut. I rolled it across a flat rock for the pleasure of it. It went straight back into the river, and I had to choose another.

volumes.title: Red Rock at Brackenford
volumes.text:
The Fells are behind me now. At Brackenford the river Ember runs under a low red cliff, and the water is the colour of weak tea with a drop of rust in it.

The cliff is sandstone. Rub it and it comes away on your palm in grains, each grain a tiny stone in its own right, worn round by some river far older than this one. A stone made of older stones: I sat on the bank a good while with that thought. Sandstone pebbles do not last. They round quickly, then crumble, and by the next bend they are sand again.

Stone five is a flat red pebble with faint ripples across one face, the very ripples you see on a sandy shallow. I have wrapped it in my spare sock, as it would not survive a journey beside the granite.

volumes.title: The Gravel Bar at Millbend
volumes.text:
Halfway, by my reckoning. At Millbend the river Ember swings wide and leaves a bar of gravel a hundred paces long, and I spent a whole morning on it like a hen in a yard.

The river sorts its stones. At the head of the bar lie cobbles as big as loaves; at the tail, gravel fine as peas. The flat ones overlap like roof tiles, all leaning into the current, so that the water presses them down rather than lifting them. I counted a hundred pebbles by kind: plenty of granite and white quartz, very little slate. The slate is being ground to mud.

Still, I found one. Stone six is a slate from the Fells, a smooth dark oval now, pleasant as a worry-stone. The shepherd who said I would find no round ones was right about his own valley, at least.

volumes.title: Flint Under Emberwick Bridge
volumes.text:
Home, for one night. The river Ember passes Emberwick under the old bridge, and a little below it my nephew works the ferry I worked for forty years. He rowed me over and I paid my penny like anyone else.

On the shoal beneath the bridge there is a stone I never noticed in all that time. The brooks from the Lowland chalk bring down flint: lumpy, white-skinned, and black as glass inside where it has broken. Flint does not wear round so much as chip. Every edge is a small, sharp, shell-shaped scar.

Stone seven is a flint the shape of a knuckle. Struck against my knife in the dusk it gave a spark, which delighted me more than a man of my years should admit. My sister says the fly-box smells of river and may stay in the porch.

volumes.title: Fairy Coins from Lode Brook
volumes.text:
A day below Emberwick, Lode Brook comes in from the limestone hills and the river Ember gains a new sort of pebble: pale grey, smooth as soap, and cool in the hand.

Look closely and some are full of little rings, each the size of a lentil with a dot in the middle. Children here call them fairy coins. A quarryman on the bank put me right. They are slices of the stems of sea-lilies, creatures kin to the starfish, which lived on a sea floor where these hills now stand. The whole pebble is made of their broken remains.

So stone eight is older than the river that carries it, and was once alive, more or less. It shows three coins on one side and five on the other. I spent them several times over in my head on the walk to the inn.

volumes.title: Black Sand at the Old Weir
volumes.text:
Below the old weir the river Ember drops what it can no longer carry. I am Barnaby Stile, ferryman retired, and today I became a prospector with a borrowed pie dish.

The trick is to swirl a scoop of sand under water and let the light grains wash over the rim. What stays behind is heavy and black. The miller's boy lent me a magnet, and half the black grains leapt to it like iron filings, which is very nearly what they are. Among the rest lay specks of deep red, no bigger than pinheads: garnets, washed out of the Fell rocks and far too small for any ring.

No gold. The miller says there never was. Compartment nine holds a twist of paper with a pinch of black sand and eleven garnets in it. I counted them twice. It is the nearest I shall come to treasure.

volumes.title: No Stones in the Marsh
volumes.text:
Three days now I have followed the river Ember through the marsh, and I have not seen a single stone. The water is brown and slow. I pushed my staff into the bed and it went down a yard without touching anything firm.

At first I felt cheated. Then the reed-cutter I am lodging with scooped up a handful of the bank and squeezed it. Grey clay, fine as flour. "That's your stones," he said. "That's where they go." He is right. The slate of Scree Beck and the soft parts of the granite have been ground so small that the river carries them as cloud, and here, where it rests, it lets them fall.

For the tenth compartment I rolled a ball of that clay and dried it by his stove. It is a marble made of mountains. It also left a grey thumbprint on my supper.

volumes.title: The Brick at Low Staithe
volumes.text:
At Low Staithe the river Ember meets the tide. Twice a day it runs backwards, which after eleven stretches of walking downstream I took rather personally.

There is a hard of pebbles below the landing, and half of them are not stones at all. I found green bottle glass frosted smooth, a blue-patterned crumb of plate, and bricks worn round as buns. The river makes no distinction. Whatever falls in, it tumbles and rounds and carries along with the rest. Among them lay the first cockle shells of the walk, and the air smelled of salt.

Number eleven is a brick pebble, orange, with a pale streak of mortar still on it. I like to think it came from the old ferry-house chimney, which fell into the Ember in my grandfather's time. If so, it has taken sixty years to come as far as I have in a fortnight.

volumes.title: Shingle at the River's Mouth
volumes.text:
The river Ember ends on the Grey Coast, slipping through a gap in a great bank of shingle and into the sea without any ceremony at all. I had expected to feel triumphant. Mostly I felt I should take my boots off, and did.

Then, among a million pebbles, I picked up a grey one speckled with black. Granite, smooth as an egg. I opened the fly-box and held it beside the sharp chip from the spring below Cold Tarn. The same stone, eighty miles apart.

I laid all twelve on a driftwood plank in their order: chip, blade, white lump, and so on down to clay, brick and egg. That is the river's whole work, set out on a plank. Tomorrow the carrier's cart takes me home to Emberwick. From the ferry bench I shall watch the water go by and know what it is carrying.

volumes.title: Eleven Empty Drawers
volumes.text:
My great-uncle Ambrose Quarrender left me his mineral cabinet. It came to the schoolhouse in Emberwick on the carrier's cart, twelve shallow drawers of walnut, and eleven of them were empty. He had sold his crystals one by one in his last winters to pay for coal, and told nobody.

Only the top drawer was full. In it lay a clear, six-sided point of quartz as long as my finger, and beside it his register: a narrow green book listing twelve specimens, each with its shape, its colour and the place he found it. Reading it was like reading the menu of a dinner already eaten.

I am Isolde Quarrender. I teach forty children their letters and know nothing of stones. But I dislike an empty drawer, and a register is very nearly a map. I intend to fill the cabinet again.

volumes.title: The Stone That Doubles
volumes.text:
The second entry in my great-uncle's register reads: "Calcite. Clear rhomb. Doubles a line of print. Lode quarry." So on Saturday I, Isolde Quarrender, schoolmistress, walked to the limestone quarry above Lode Brook and asked the foreman if I might look through his rubbish.

He was very civil about it. Calcite fills the cracks in limestone, white and glassy, and when struck it breaks always into the same leaning block, like a brick someone has pushed sideways. Most pieces are cloudy. The foreman's boy found me a clear one the size of a sugar lump.

At home I laid it on the register and my uncle's thin handwriting appeared twice, one line floating just above the other. I turned the crystal and the second line walked round the first. The children will not believe it on Monday. I scarcely believe it now, and I am looking straight at it.

volumes.title: Fool's Gold
volumes.text:
Tobias Wren, aged nine, came into my schoolroom in Emberwick on Tuesday convinced that he was rich. He had split a roofing slate behind his father's shed and found gold in it: three bright cubes, sharp-cornered, shining like new brass.

I opened my great-uncle's register to the third entry. "Pyrite. Cubes, brassy, faces finely lined. Common in slate. Not gold." Ambrose Quarrender had underlined the last two words, I suspect from experience. We tried the test he gives. Gold leaves a golden streak on unglazed china; Tobias's treasure, rubbed on the back of a saucer, left a streak of greenish black.

He bore it well. What astonished us both was the shape. Nobody carved those cubes. They grew that way in the dark, square on every side. Tobias has sold me one for sixpence and a mention in the register, and Drawer Three is filled.

volumes.title: Purple from the Spoil Heap
volumes.text:
Entry four in the Quarrender register, which I am refilling drawer by drawer, says: "Fluorspar. Cubes, violet. Old lead workings, Ravel Fell." It is nine miles from Emberwick to Ravel Fell, and I walked them in my second-best boots.

The old miners threw fluorspar away. It came up with the lead ore and was no use to them, so the waste heaps below the levels are speckled with it, glassy and pale. Most is broken. After two hours on my knees I found a lump with three perfect cubes standing on it, the colour of watered blackcurrant, each edge as long as my thumbnail.

My great-uncle notes that a cube of fluorspar, tapped just so, splits off its corners and becomes an eight-sided shape like two pyramids joined. I do not intend to try. It took me a whole Saturday to find one with its corners on.

volumes.title: Swallow-Tails in the Clay
volumes.text:
The brickworks in the Lowlands digs its clay from a pit as deep as a church, and the men there keep a shelf of oddities the spade turns up. My great-uncle's register sent me to them. Entry five: "Gypsum. Clear blades, twinned like a swallow's tail. Clay pits. Soft."

Soft is the word. The foreman handed me a crystal as long as my hand, shaped like an arrowhead where two blades had grown together. "Try your nail on it," he said. I did, and my thumbnail left a scratch. A stone I can mark with my own finger!

It is the same stuff, he told me, that is baked and ground to make plaster. I carried it home to Emberwick wrapped in my scarf. Drawer Five now holds something that looks like ice and will never melt, provided no pupil of mine tests it with a thumb.

volumes.title: Garnets in the Garden Wall
volumes.text:
I have walked many miles this year refilling my great-uncle Ambrose's crystal cabinet, so it was humbling to find entry six in the wall of my own schoolhouse garden.

The register says: "Garnet. Twelve-faced, dark red. In glittering grey schist." The wall is built of that very rock, carted down from the Fells a century ago. I had taken the lumps in it for rust. They are crystals, dark as old port, each about the size of a pea. Where one has weathered free you can count the faces, every one a neat diamond shape. I made it twelve. So did the three children helping me, eventually.

A loose stone by the gate gave up two. One is in Drawer Six. The other I have kept back, on the advice of a note in my uncle's margin: "Always keep a spare. Collectors trade."

volumes.title: The Heaviest Drawer
volumes.text:
Entry seven of the Quarrender register is a stone I could not have found alone. "Galena. Lead ore. Cubes, bright grey. Very heavy." It lies underground, in the lead veins of the Northern Fells, and schoolmistresses are not encouraged down mines.

So I wrote to a mine captain. His reply came to Emberwick in a tobacco tin, and inside, in sawdust, lay a cluster of cubes like a handful of tiny silver dice. New-broken galena is as bright as a mirror. It dulls in time to the grey of a rainy sky, and he had cracked this piece fresh for me.

What the register cannot convey is the weight. It is no bigger than a plum, and when I passed it round the class every child's hand dropped. "It's cheating," said one. Drawer Seven needed a second nail in its runner.

volumes.title: What the Fair Brought Back
volumes.text:
At the autumn fair in Emberwick a man sells stones from a barrow: polished pebbles, shark's teeth, and rough grey balls he cracks open for a penny. I went looking for entry eight in my great-uncle's register. "Amethyst. Quartz, violet. Points lining a hollow stone."

He had one: half a grey ball the size of a teacup, and inside it a cave of purple crystals, six-sided, deepest in colour at the tips. I paid three shillings without bargaining, which he seemed to find disappointing.

At home I turned it over. On the underside was a paper label, brown with age, in a hand like spider thread: "A.Q. No. 8." It is not one like my uncle's. It is my uncle's. It has travelled for years between his coal bill and that barrow, and now it sits in Drawer Eight, where its outline is still pressed in the felt.

volumes.title: Black Needles in Granite
volumes.text:
Nine drawers. I am Isolde Quarrender, and I have nearly refilled my great-uncle's crystal cabinet, but entry nine cost me three visits to the granite quarry on the Fell road before I knew what I was looking at.

"Tourmaline. Black. Long three-sided prisms, grooved lengthwise." I had been stepping over it. In the coarse veins of the granite lie black rods, thin as knitting needles, and I had taken them for coal. Coal, though, is soft and dirties the fingers. These are harder than a knife, and every one is scored along its length like a stick of liquorice. Break one across and the end is a rounded triangle.

The quarrymen call it "schorl" and curse it for spoiling good stone. One of them split out a needle two inches long for me, and would take nothing for it but my opinion of his daughter's spelling.

volumes.title: A Book with Glass Pages
volumes.text:
The tenth entry in my great-uncle's register pleased my class in Emberwick more than all the others together. "Mica. Six-sided book of leaves. Splits for ever."

I found it at the granite quarry, in the same coarse vein that gave me the black tourmaline: a silvery block as wide as a penny and half as thick, with six flat sides. It is a crystal that grows in sheets. Slide a pin under the edge and a leaf lifts off, clear, bendable and thinner than paper. Split that leaf and you have two. The children halved and halved again until the pieces floated on their breath.

Old stoves, I am told, have mica in their doors, because it does not mind the fire. I gave the class the loose leaves and kept the book. Drawer Ten is filled. Two remain, and the register's hand grows shakier toward the end.

volumes.title: The Dairy Doorstop
volumes.text:
Entry eleven nearly defeated me. "Heavy spar. White crested blades, like a cock's comb. Heavy as its name." My great-uncle found his in a mine long since flooded, and I had no notion where to find another.

I offered my spare garnet in trade to anyone who could help. On Thursday little Ada Furlong arrived at the schoolhouse in Emberwick pulling a handcart. In it sat a white lump the size of a loaf, all ridged plates standing on edge. "Gran says it has held the dairy door open for thirty years," she said, "and you may have it, for it stubs everyone's toes."

It is heavy spar beyond doubt. A stone that looks like chalk has no business weighing so much. It will not fit the drawer, so I chipped off one good crest for the cabinet. The rest holds open the schoolroom door, and stubs toes there instead.

volumes.title: Grown on the Windowsill
volumes.text:
The last entry in my great-uncle Ambrose's register is the shortest. "Salt. Cubes. Grown on the kitchen windowsill, one winter. The only one I made myself."

So the twelfth crystal could not be found, bought or begged. I stirred kitchen salt into warm water until no more would vanish, hung a thread in the jar, and set it on the schoolhouse sill. Then I waited, which I do badly. In a week the thread was gritty. In five, a cube the size of a pea hung there, square-cornered, and nobody had shaped it.

It lies in Drawer Twelve, in a pillbox. The cabinet is full again: eleven journeys and one jar. There were blank pages left in the green book. Tonight I ruled a line beneath his last entry and wrote, in my own hand, "No. 13." The rest of the line is empty yet.

volumes.title: Kestrel Level
volumes.text:
I am Edmund Rook, captain of Kestrel Level, a lead mine driven into the side of Ravel Fell in the Northern Fells. "Captain" is only what miners call the man who must decide where to dig. I have eleven men, two ponies and a boy called Tam, who pushes the ore tubs and asks questions.

Our ore is galena, bright grey and heavy, the stuff lead is smelted from. It lies in a vein we call the Silver Rake: a crack in the limestone, nearly upright, filled long ago with minerals. The level follows it into the hill for four hundred fathoms. Parts were dug before anyone kept records. We call those miners "the old man" and find his pick-marks everywhere.

The owners in Emberwick want a day-book kept of ore and veins. I begin it this first Monday of the year, with the vein three feet wide and good.

volumes.title: What a Vein Is Made Of
volumes.text:
Tam, the tub-boy at Kestrel Level, asked me today why the whole hill is not lead. A fair question. I am the mine's captain and ought to have an answer.

A vein is a healed crack. Ages ago the limestone of Ravel Fell split, and hot waters rising through the split left minerals on its walls, layer upon layer, until it was full. Most of the filling is no use to us. There is white calcite, glassy fluorspar, and heavy spar like lumps of chalk. Miners lump all these together as "gangue" and throw them on the heap.

The galena runs through the middle in ribs: here a thread, there a band as thick as my arm. I held the candle close and showed Tam the layers, like the rings of a cut onion. He said the hill had been mended with treasure. I shall not better that.

volumes.title: The Dressing Floor
volumes.text:
Nothing comes out of Kestrel Level clean. What the ponies draw from the hill is a grey rubble of ore and waste together, and it must be parted on the dressing floor beside the beck before the smelter will look at it.

The secret is weight. Galena is far heavier than the spar it grows in. So the lumps are broken small with flat hammers, then shaken in a sieve under water. The heavy ore sinks to the bottom of the sieve and the light waste rides on top to be skimmed away. The finest sludge is washed down a sloping trough, where the lead settles first.

It is cold, wet work, done mostly by the miners' wives and sisters in clogs. In this day-book I, Edmund Rook, captain, record eleven tons of dressed ore for the month, and that Widow Marl can judge a sieve by ear.

volumes.title: The Vein Pinches
volumes.text:
A bad week to write up. At four hundred and six fathoms from the entrance of Kestrel Level, the Silver Rake has begun to pinch.

Veins do this. The crack that holds the ore was never an even width, and where its walls draw together the filling thins. In March we were cutting galena three feet across. Today the vein is a hand's breadth of white spar with a grey thread in it no thicker than a bootlace. The men call it "nipped". We drive on through it and hope that it opens again, as it has before.

Old Abel Dunnock, who has worked this hill for fifty years, put his palm flat on the rock and said nothing, which worried me more than talk would have. As captain I have ordered the forehead driven six feet more. Tam has stopped asking questions, and I find I miss them.

volumes.title: Signs on the Fell Top
volumes.text:
With the vein at Kestrel Level pinched to a thread, I left the men driving and spent two days on top of Ravel Fell with my eyes on the turf. A mine captain does half his prospecting above ground.

A vein shows at the surface if you know its manners. Where the Silver Rake runs beneath, there is a line of shallow hollows left by the old man's first diggings, and molehills there throw up crumbs of spar. Better still is the leadwort, a small white flower that thrives on ground too full of lead for grass. Follow the flowers and you follow the vein.

I followed them east for half a mile. Then, above the spot where we are now digging, they stopped dead, and began again forty paces to the north. I have drawn it in the day-book. I do not yet know what it means.

volumes.title: The Wall of Clay
volumes.text:
Today, at four hundred and eight fathoms, Kestrel Level ran into a wall. The thread of ore we have been nursing for weeks ends against a smooth, sloping face of rock smeared with grey clay, and beyond it is nothing but barren shale.

It is a fault. At some time after our vein was made, Ravel Fell cracked again along this line, and one side of the hill slid past the other. The Silver Rake was cut in two like a ribbon with scissors. Our half stops here. The other half is somewhere beyond the clay, carried up, down or sideways, and nobody can see through rock.

Abel Dunnock held his candle to the wall and whistled. The surface is polished like a table and scored with fine straight grooves. "The hill wrote down which way it went," he said. I, Edmund Rook, captain, intend to learn to read it.

volumes.title: Reading the Grooves
volumes.text:
The question at Kestrel Level is simple to ask. Our vein of lead ore has been cut off by a fault, and the lost half lies to the left of us or to the right. Guess wrong, and we tunnel away from it until the money is gone.

Abel Dunnock and I spent the shift with our noses to the fault wall. The grooves on it run nearly level, so the ground slid sideways, not up or down. Abel stroked the face with his palm: smooth one way, catching the other, like a cat's fur. Rock, he says, feels smooth in the direction the far side travelled. Smooth to the north.

Then I remembered the leadwort on the fell top, which broke off above this spot and began again forty paces northward. Two witnesses agree. I have written in the day-book, as captain: we turn north.

volumes.title: The Crosscut
volumes.text:
A tunnel driven across the grain of the ground to find a vein is called a crosscut, and ours at Kestrel Level now runs northward from the fault where the Silver Rake was lost. I measure it every Saturday with a knotted cord.

It is slow. The shale is tough and gives us nothing to sell. Two men at the forehead bore holes with hammer and steel, a quarter-turn to each blow, then fire a small charge of powder and wait for the smoke to clear. A good week is five feet. Tam trams the waste out and has learned to tell good air from bad by the candle flame, which leans and yellows when the air grows poor.

Eleven weeks, forty-nine feet, not one speck of ore. I am Edmund Rook, captain, and I write the figures down plainly, because the owners in Emberwick can add.

volumes.title: Water in the Level
volumes.text:
It rained on Ravel Fell for nine days, and on the tenth Kestrel Level filled to the knee. Every mine is a drain for the hill above it. Water finds the old man's forgotten workings, gathers there, and comes down on us through cracks we never knew of.

Our level slopes toward its mouth, so that water runs out along a channel under the rails. This week the channel choked with silt and the crosscut became a pond. No one was in any danger. The men cannot bore holes under water, and for six days my company did nothing but dig silt, mend the channel and say what they thought of the weather.

Tam floated a candle stub on a chip of wood to watch which way the water wanted to go. It was sensible, so I have entered it in the day-book: "Drainage surveyed by T., boat."

volumes.title: Green Stain and Black Jack
volumes.text:
Sixty-one feet into the crosscut at Kestrel Level, and the rock has changed at last. I write this with my hands still dirty.

First came a green stain on the wall, bright as a mallard's head. That is copper showing, and beside it a few brassy specks of copper ore, too little to pay for the candle we saw it by. Then a string of spar carrying dark brown crystals with a resinous shine. The men groaned. It is zinc blende, which miners call "black jack", for it looks like lead ore to a hopeful eye and the smelter will not take it.

Still, Abel Dunnock was cheerful. Stains and strings do not wander alone in dead ground, he says. They are the fringe of something. As captain I ought to be cautious in the day-book, so I record only this: the shale is no longer barren.

volumes.title: One More Month
volumes.text:
The owners of Kestrel Level met in Emberwick on Thursday, in the back room of the corn exchange, and I, Edmund Rook, went down from Ravel Fell in a clean collar to explain why their mine had sold no ore since midsummer.

I took the day-book and three things in my pockets: a piece of the last good galena, a chip of the green-stained rock, and the assayer's note on our old ore, which shows a little silver in every ton of lead. I laid them on the table and told the story straight. A vein cut by a fault. A crosscut going north. Seventy feet driven, and signs.

They are a draper, a miller, two farmers and a clergyman's widow, and the widow asked the best questions. They voted me one more month of wages and powder. Not a week over. I walked home in the dark, counting feet.

volumes.title: The Vein Regained
volumes.text:
On the nineteenth day of our last month, at eighty-three feet in the crosscut, the borer at the forehead of Kestrel Level felt his steel jump into something soft. He shouted. I was there before the echo.

We cleared the face by hand. White spar first, then a rib of grey so bright that Tam said somebody had left a mirror in the hill. It is the Silver Rake, the vein we lost at the fault, carried north just as the grooves and the leadwort said. By Saturday we had it measured: two feet of solid galena, standing upright and running on eastward.

Abel Dunnock laid his palm on it and this time he spoke. "There you are," he said, as if to a strayed ewe. I have put a lump the size of a plum in my pocket and closed this day-book. The next one starts Monday.

volumes.title: What a Pebble Is
volumes.text:
This primer was written on the beach at Tarrow, on the Grey Coast, by me, Dorcas Whin, for my nephew Kit, who came to stay for the summer with one bucket and a great many questions. I have set down twelve lessons, one for each week he was here.

Lesson the first: a pebble is a piece of rock that water has rolled until its corners are gone. Smaller than a pea, we call it grit. Bigger than your fist, it is a cobble. Everything in between is a pebble, and a beach like ours holds more of them than there are people in the world.

Kit's first question was whether any had holes in. A stone with a hole right through it is lucky, his friend says. I told him yes, somewhere, and that learning the others would pass the time while we looked.

volumes.title: Wet Stones and Dry Stones
volumes.text:
Second lesson from the beach at Tarrow, where my nephew Kit and I are learning pebbles one week at a time.

On Monday he filled his bucket at the water's edge with the finest stones he had ever seen: deep red, bottle green, black with gold flecks. By supper they sat on the windowsill, dry, and every one had turned the same dusty grey. He thought someone had swapped them.

Nobody had. A dry pebble is covered in scratches that scatter the light and hide its colour. Water fills the scratches and the colour shows through, just as a wet pavement is darker than a dry one. So here is the rule: always judge a pebble wet. Carry a jar of water, or do as Kit does and lick your thumb. To get his red stone back, we dropped it in a glass. It sits by his bed, glowing.

volumes.title: Hard and Soft
volumes.text:
Third lesson of the Pebble Primer, set down at Tarrow by Dorcas Whin, aunt, with Kit, nephew, doing the scratching.

Stones differ in hardness, and you may sort them with three tools you already own. First, your fingernail: if it scratches the pebble, the stone is very soft, like chalk. Second, a copper coin, which marks limestone but not much else. Third, a steel nail. Flint and quartz laugh at steel; the nail leaves only a silvery line of itself, which rubs off. (An aunt should hold the nail.)

Kit lined up his week's pebbles from softest to hardest along the sea wall, eleven in a row, and it took him the whole afternoon. The chalk he could write with. The white quartz at the far end scratched the glass of my jam jar, which I had not planned on. He looked at every one for holes. None yet.

volumes.title: Three Families of Stone
volumes.text:
Fourth lesson, written at the kitchen table in Tarrow because it rained, with a tray of pebbles between my nephew Kit and me.

Every pebble on the beach belongs to one of three families. The fire-made stones were once melted, deep underground, and cooled into a mass of crystals: granite is one. The laid-down stones were once mud, sand or shells, settled in layers under water and pressed hard: sandstone, limestone and chalk. The changed stones began as either sort and were squeezed and baked inside mountains until they turned into something new, like slate, which was once mud.

How to tell? Look close. Crystals locked together, speckled all through: fire-made. Grains or layers: laid-down. Stripes, bands or a glittery sheen: changed. Kit sorted forty pebbles into three saucers and got thirty-one right. I got thirty-four, and he checked.

volumes.title: Granite, the Speckled One
volumes.text:
Fifth lesson of the Primer. On the beach at Tarrow my nephew Kit has a favourite kind of pebble, pink and grey and speckled like a thrush's egg, so this week we looked at it properly. It is granite.

Granite is three things mixed, and with a reading-glass you can find all three. The grey, glassy grains are quartz. The pink or cream blocks, which sometimes show a flat shining face, are feldspar. The black flecks that glitter when you tilt the stone are mica. Wet the pebble first.

Granite was molten once and cooled slowly, far underground, which gave the crystals time to grow big enough to see. There is no granite cliff near Tarrow. Kit's pebbles have come a long way, down rivers or along the shore, to end up in his bucket. He approves. He came a long way himself, on the carrier's cart.

volumes.title: Sandstone and Its Layers
volumes.text:
Sixth lesson, from Dorcas Whin's primer for her nephew Kit, written halfway through our summer on the beach at Tarrow.

Pick up a pebble that feels rough, like a nutmeg grater. Rub two together and grains fall off. That is sandstone, and it is exactly what it says: sand, laid down by water, then glued and pressed into rock. Under the reading-glass you see the grains packed like sugar in a lump. Often there are stripes, pale and dark, thin as the pages of a shut book. Each stripe is a layer of sand that settled, perhaps in a single flood.

Kit found a red pebble with nine stripes and worked out that he was holding nine floods in one hand. So a beach is sand that became stone and is becoming sand again. We sat and listened to the waves doing it. It makes a hissing noise.

volumes.title: Flint, the Glassy One
volumes.text:
Seventh lesson. The cliffs east of Tarrow are white chalk, and from them come the oddest pebbles on our beach. My nephew Kit calls them "the potatoes".

They are flints: knobbly lumps with a white, chalky skin. A whole one is dull. But find one the sea has broken, and inside it is dark, smooth and shiny as a bottle, grey or brown or nearly black. Flint breaks like glass, in curved scoops with sharp edges, so here is the one safety rule of this primer: we never smash flints, and we mind our fingers on fresh ones.

Long ago people chipped flint into knives and arrowheads because of those edges. And two flints tapped together in the dusk will give a spark and a strange burnt smell. Kit and I tried it behind the boat-shed. Many flints have hollows in them, but, he reports, no holes right through.

volumes.title: The Ring Around the Stone
volumes.text:
Eighth lesson of the Pebble Primer, by Dorcas Whin. This one began when Kit ran up the beach at Tarrow holding a grey pebble with a white line all the way round it, like string round a parcel.

That line is a vein of quartz. Long before the pebble was a pebble, it was part of a bed of rock, and the rock cracked. Water seeped through the crack carrying dissolved quartz, and left it there until the crack was filled with white. Later the rock broke up, the sea rounded the pieces, and here is one with its mended crack still showing.

Quartz is harder than the grey stone, so the white line stands up like a ridge you can feel with your eyes shut. Fishermen's children here call a stone with an unbroken ring a wishing stone. Kit wished at once. I can guess for what.

volumes.title: Pebbles That Were Alive
volumes.text:
Ninth lesson. Some of the pale grey pebbles at Tarrow have shapes in them, and this week my nephew Kit learned to find them: curved white lines like fingernail parings, tiny coils, and patterns like the bottom of a wicker basket.

They are fossils. The grey stone is limestone, which was once the muddy floor of a warm sea, and the shapes are the shells and corals of creatures that lived there, buried and turned to stone along with the mud. The curved lines are shells seen edge-on. The basket pattern is coral.

There is a kitchen test for limestone. Put a drop of vinegar on the pebble and watch through a reading-glass: it fizzes, very gently. Nothing else on the beach does that except chalk and seashells, which are made of the same stuff. Kit has vinegared everything in the house, including, I regret to say, the doorstep.

volumes.title: The Impostors
volumes.text:
Tenth lesson, set down at Tarrow by Dorcas Whin for her nephew Kit, who was fooled four times this week and enjoyed it.

Not everything rounded on a beach is a stone. The sea will tumble anything. That frosted green pebble is the bottom of a bottle. The orange one with little holes is brick. The white one with a blue flower on it was a plate. The black one that marks your fingers is coal. And the honey-coloured piece that feels warm and weighs almost nothing may be amber, which is tree resin turned hard, though Kit's proved to be a boiled sweet.

How to know them: glass shows no grains at all, brick is full of bubbles, pottery has a skin of glaze on one side only. We keep the impostors in their own jar. Kit says it is the prettiest jar we have.

volumes.title: How the Sea Sorts
volumes.text:
Eleventh lesson, from the last full week of my nephew Kit's summer at Tarrow.

Walk from the water's edge to the top of the beach and watch your feet. Down by the waves the pebbles are small and the sand begins. Higher up they grow larger, and at the very top lies the storm ridge, a bank of big stones that only the winter gales can throw so far. The sea is a sorter. Shape is sorted too. Flat pebbles ride the wash like little plates and collect in drifts. Those are the ones for skimming: thin, round, and fitting the crook of your finger. Kit's best is seven bounces, and mine is nine.

He has searched every drift for a stone with a hole. One week is left. I have told him honestly that some summers do not have one in them.

volumes.title: The Holed Stone
volumes.text:
Twelfth and last lesson of the Pebble Primer. On his final morning at Tarrow my nephew Kit went down to the low-tide rocks, and came back up the beach walking very carefully, as though carrying an egg.

It was a grey limestone pebble with a hole clean through it, big enough for his little finger. I, Dorcas Whin, who have lived here thirty years, own only two. And here is the lesson: such holes are made by a small shellfish called a piddock, which bores into soft rock and lives in the tunnel. When the rock breaks up and the sea rounds the pieces, some still carry the empty burrow. So Kit's lucky stone was once somebody's house.

He threaded it on string and tipped the rest of his bucket back for the next learner. That is the primer's last rule: learn all of them, keep one.
